title: Race as a Social Construction
description: Why race is real in its consequences but not biological in its foundations

concepts.title: The Biological Critique of Race
concepts.contentHtml:
Sociologists and biologists overwhelmingly reject the idea that race is a natural biological category. The 1998 American Anthropological Association Statement on Race declares that human populations cannot be sorted into discrete biological races: roughly 94% of human genetic variation lies within conventionally recognized racial groups, and only about 6% between them (Lewontin 1972).

Skin colour, hair texture, and facial features vary continuously across geography — a pattern called clinal variation. There is no genetic marker present in all members of one 'race' and absent in all others. The traits used to classify race in the United States differ sharply from those used in Brazil, South Africa, or Japan, which makes sense only if races are cultural categories projected onto bodies, not natural kinds discovered in them.

This does not mean race is unreal — it means race is real as a social fact, with measurable effects on housing, schooling, policing, health, and wealth. The slogan, drawing on the Thomas theorem, is that race is 'a fiction with material consequences.'

concepts.title: Race Versus Ethnicity
concepts.contentHtml:
Sociologists distinguish race from ethnicity, although the two often overlap and bleed into one another in practice.

Race typically refers to a socially constructed category based on perceived physical differences — phenotype, skin colour, ancestry — that is imposed from outside as much as claimed from within. Racial categories tend to be hierarchically ranked and historically rooted in conquest, slavery, and colonial administration.

Ethnicity typically refers to shared cultural heritage — language, religion, national origin, customs, kinship — and is more often claimed by the group itself. Irish Americans, Hmong, Igbo, and Ashkenazi Jews are ethnic groups; their members may belong to one or more racial categories depending on context.

Max Weber defined ethnic groups as 'human groups that entertain a subjective belief in their common descent.' The belief, not the descent, does the social work. Ethnic boundaries are also constructed and shift over time — Italians, Irish, and Jews in the US were not always coded as 'white.'

concepts.title: The Social Construction Thesis
concepts.contentHtml:
To say race is socially constructed is to make several claims at once.

First, the categories are constructed: which traits count as racially significant, how many races there are, and where the lines fall are products of history, law, and politics rather than biology. The US 'one-drop rule', Brazil's hundreds of colour terms, and the South African apartheid registry illustrate how differently the same human variation can be carved up.

Second, the meanings attached to categories are constructed: stereotypes, hierarchies, and associations are produced and reproduced by institutions, media, and everyday interaction.

Third, the consequences are real: constructed categories shape who is policed, who is hired, who lives where, and who lives how long. As Karen Fields and Barbara Fields argue in Racecraft (2012), racism is not the product of race but its source — discriminatory practice creates the categories it claims to discover.

title: The Historical Formation of Race
description: How modern racial categories were forged by colonialism, slavery, and pseudo-science

concepts.title: Colonialism and Chattel Slavery
concepts.contentHtml:
The modern concept of race is historically recent. Ancient and medieval societies certainly distinguished insiders from outsiders, but the idea of fixed, biologically inherited racial groups arranged in a hierarchy crystallised between roughly 1500 and 1800 alongside European colonial expansion and the Atlantic slave trade.

In the seventeenth-century Chesapeake, English, Irish, and African labourers initially worked under similar conditions of indenture. Following uprisings such as Bacon's Rebellion (1676), colonial legislatures gradually passed laws — the Virginia slave codes of 1705 are a key example — that hardened a distinction between hereditary 'Negro' slavery and free 'white' labour.

This was a political settlement, not a biological discovery. As the historian Barbara Fields argues, race was invented to explain why the freedoms claimed under Enlightenment principles could be denied to enslaved Africans. The invention of whiteness as a property and a privilege (Cheryl Harris 1993) was inseparable from the invention of Blackness as its subordinated counterpart.

concepts.title: Scientific Racism and Eugenics
concepts.contentHtml:
From the eighteenth century onward, European scholars sought a scientific grounding for racial hierarchy. Carl Linnaeus's Systema Naturae (1758) divided humans into four varieties with attached temperaments. Johann Blumenbach (1795) coined 'Caucasian' for what he considered the most beautiful skull type. Samuel Morton in the 1830s measured cranial capacities to argue for white superiority — work later shown by Stephen Jay Gould (The Mismeasure of Man, 1981) to be riddled with bias.

By the late nineteenth century, scientific racism fused with social Darwinism and the new statistics of Francis Galton to produce eugenics: the project of improving the human stock by encouraging 'fit' reproduction and discouraging or preventing the 'unfit.' The United States passed compulsory sterilisation laws (upheld in Buck v. Bell, 1927) that sterilised over 60,000 people, mainly poor women and people of colour.

Nazi Germany pushed eugenic logic to genocide. After the Holocaust, UNESCO's 1950 Statement on Race formally repudiated the biological race concept, though the underlying ideas have proven stubborn.

concepts.title: Jim Crow and the Long Civil Rights Era
concepts.contentHtml:
Emancipation in 1865 did not produce racial equality. After Reconstruction collapsed in 1877, Southern states erected the system of Jim Crow: legally mandated segregation of schools, transport, hospitals, restrooms, cemeteries, and water fountains, enforced by disenfranchisement laws (poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses) and by lynching.

The Supreme Court legitimated segregation in Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) under the doctrine of 'separate but equal.' In practice, Black facilities were systematically underfunded. Federal housing policy in the 1930s — the Home Owners' Loan Corporation's redlining maps and FHA underwriting standards — extended segregation into Northern cities by denying mortgages in Black neighbourhoods.

The civil rights movement dismantled formal Jim Crow: Brown v. Board (1954), the 1964 Civil Rights Act, the 1965 Voting Rights Act, and the 1968 Fair Housing Act. But sociologists such as Douglas Massey emphasise that the legal end of segregation did not undo decades of accumulated disadvantage in wealth, schooling, and place — a phenomenon sometimes called the 'long shadow' of slavery and Jim Crow.

title: Classical Theorists of Race
description: Du Bois, Cox, and the Chicago school on the colour line

concepts.title: W.E.B. Du Bois and the Colour Line
concepts.contentHtml:
W.E.B. Du Bois (1868–1963) is increasingly recognised as a founder of American sociology. His The Philadelphia Negro (1899) is one of the discipline's first systematic urban ethnographies, combining door-to-door survey work, mapping, and historical analysis to study the city's Seventh Ward.

In The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Du Bois announced that 'the problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the colour line' — a global structural division that organised politics, economics, and identity. He introduced double consciousness: the experience of 'always looking at one's self through the eyes of others,' of feeling 'two-ness — an American, a Negro; two souls, two thoughts, two unreconciled strivings.'

Du Bois later argued in Black Reconstruction (1935) that white workers accepted a 'public and psychological wage' of whiteness in exchange for cross-class solidarity with white elites — an early structural analysis of how race divides the working class.

concepts.title: Oliver Cox: Race, Caste, Class
concepts.contentHtml:
Oliver Cromwell Cox (1901–1974), in Caste, Class, and Race (1948), produced one of the first systematic Marxist analyses of racism. Cox attacked the prevailing 'caste school' (Lloyd Warner, John Dollard) which described the US South as a caste system analogous to India.

Cox argued the analogy was misleading. Indian caste, he claimed, was a stable religiously sanctioned status order; American racial hierarchy was a modern, dynamic, conflictual system tied to capitalism. Racism, in his view, originated with the European exploitation of darker-skinned labour for plantation production. It was not a holdover from primitive prejudice but a capitalist invention that justified colonial exploitation.

Cox's emphasis on the political economy of racism prefigures later work by William Julius Wilson on race and class, by world-systems theorists on the racialised division of labour, and by 'racial capitalism' scholarship after Cedric Robinson's Black Marxism (1983).

concepts.title: The Chicago School and the Race Relations Cycle
concepts.contentHtml:
The early-twentieth-century Chicago school of sociology, centred on Robert E. Park and Ernest Burgess, made race a central topic of urban research. Park, a former secretary to Booker T. Washington, proposed in 1926 a race relations cycle with four stages: contact, competition, accommodation, and assimilation.

On Park's account, when groups meet, they compete for jobs and territory; eventually conflict gives way to a working modus vivendi (accommodation) and finally to a merging of cultures and identities (assimilation). The cycle was 'apparently progressive and irreversible.'

The model was hugely influential but heavily criticised. It assumed that the receiving society — typically white, Protestant, middle-class America — was a neutral standard rather than itself a racial project. It underestimated how persistently the 'colour line' blocked assimilation for African Americans. Later sociologists such as Milton Gordon (Assimilation in American Life, 1964) refined the model into seven sub-processes; still later work moved toward more pluralist and structural accounts.

title: Racial Formation and Critical Race Theory
description: Race as political project; structural racism, intersectionality, and colourblind ideology

concepts.title: Omi and Winant's Racial Formation
concepts.contentHtml:
Michael Omi and Howard Winant's Racial Formation in the United States (1986; revised 1994 and 2014) became the dominant sociological theory of race in the late twentieth century. They define racial formation as 'the sociohistorical process by which racial categories are created, inhabited, transformed, and destroyed.'

Their central concept is the racial project: any effort to interpret, represent, or explain racial dynamics, and to redistribute resources along racial lines. Racial projects can be governmental (the US Census, immigration law), institutional (university admissions), cultural (films, music), or quotidian (street-level interaction).

Omi and Winant criticise approaches that reduce race to ethnicity, class, or nation. Race, they argue, is an autonomous axis of social organisation that articulates with — but cannot be reduced to — these others. Their framework helped move sociology beyond the prejudice-and-discrimination paradigm toward a focus on how state policy, ideology, and social movements continually make and remake race.

concepts.title: Critical Race Theory and Intersectionality
concepts.contentHtml:
Critical Race Theory (CRT) emerged in US legal scholarship in the late 1970s and 1980s through the work of Derrick Bell, Kimberlé Crenshaw, Richard Delgado, Patricia Williams, and others. Several propositions are widely shared: that racism is ordinary rather than aberrant in American life; that formal legal equality often coexists with substantive inequality; and that interest convergence (Bell) explains why civil rights gains tend to come when they also serve white interests.

Crenshaw's 1989 paper 'Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex' coined intersectionality: the idea that systems of oppression — race, gender, class, sexuality — combine in ways not captured by any single axis. Black women's experiences of discrimination, she argued, are erased by anti-discrimination doctrine that treats race and sex as separate, mutually exclusive categories.

Sociologists have extended intersectional analysis to studies of work, health, policing, and family life. Patricia Hill Collins's Black Feminist Thought (1990) frames intersectionality as a matrix of domination in which intersecting oppressions also produce distinctive standpoints and forms of resistance.

concepts.title: Colourblind Racism and Structural Racism
concepts.contentHtml:
After the dismantling of legal segregation, overt expressions of racial supremacy became socially unacceptable in mainstream US discourse. Sociologists asked whether racism had ended or merely changed form.

Eduardo Bonilla-Silva's Racism Without Racists (first edition 2003) argues for the latter. He identifies a dominant ideology of colourblind racism built around four frames: abstract liberalism (using equal-opportunity rhetoric to oppose remedies for inequality); naturalisation (segregation reflects natural preferences); cultural racism (group disparities are due to cultural deficits); and minimisation (racism is no longer a major problem). Together these frames let speakers defend racial inequality without using racial language.

Closely related is the concept of structural or systemic racism (Joe Feagin): racial disparities are produced not mainly by individual prejudice but by the cumulative operation of housing, education, criminal justice, and labour market institutions that were historically designed in racially biased ways and remain so even when their formal rules are race-neutral.

title: Inequality, Prejudice, and Intergroup Relations
description: Contact, audit studies, segregation, the racial wealth gap, and mass incarceration

concepts.title: Allport, Contact, and the Audit Study
concepts.contentHtml:
Gordon Allport's The Nature of Prejudice (1954) is the foundational social-psychological text. Allport defined prejudice as 'an antipathy based upon a faulty and inflexible generalization' and proposed the contact hypothesis: prejudice declines when groups have sustained contact under four conditions — equal status, common goals, intergroup cooperation, and the support of authorities, law, or custom.

A meta-analysis by Pettigrew and Tropp (2006) covering 515 studies found that contact does generally reduce prejudice, though the effect size varies and the optimal conditions are not always met.

For studying discrimination rather than attitudes, sociologists use audit studies. Bertrand and Mullainathan's 'Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal?' (2004) sent 5,000 fictitious résumés with randomly assigned Black-sounding or white-sounding names to job ads in Boston and Chicago. White-sounding names received 50% more callbacks. Pager (2003) showed that white men with felony records received more callbacks than Black men without records. These designs isolate the causal effect of perceived race.

concepts.title: Residential Segregation and the Wealth Gap
concepts.contentHtml:
Douglas Massey and Nancy Denton's American Apartheid (1993) documented that, even decades after the Fair Housing Act, African Americans in major US metros lived under conditions of hypersegregation: extreme separation across multiple geographic dimensions. This was not simply the product of preference or poverty; it had been engineered by redlining, racially restrictive covenants, blockbusting, exclusionary zoning, and steering by real-estate agents.

Segregation matters because place determines schooling, exposure to environmental hazards, access to jobs, and the security of one's largest asset — the home.

This produces the racial wealth gap. Melvin Oliver and Thomas Shapiro's Black Wealth/White Wealth (1995) showed that the median Black household holds a small fraction of the wealth of the median white household, and that the gap is much larger than the income gap because wealth accumulates across generations through inheritance, home equity, and access to credit. Twenty-first-century Federal Reserve data continue to show median white household wealth roughly six to ten times median Black household wealth.

concepts.title: Mass Incarceration and Segmented Assimilation
concepts.contentHtml:
Michelle Alexander's The New Jim Crow (2010) argues that the post-1970 expansion of US incarceration — from roughly 350,000 prisoners in 1972 to over two million by 2010 — has functioned as a racialised system of social control. The 'War on Drugs' targeted Black and Latino neighbourhoods despite similar drug use rates across groups, and a felony record carries lifelong civil penalties: in many states the loss of voting rights, exclusion from jury service, public housing, and many forms of employment.

Sociologists Bruce Western and Becky Pettit show that by the 2000s, Black men without high-school degrees had a roughly 70% lifetime probability of imprisonment.

For immigrant groups, the picture is different. Alejandro Portes and Min Zhou's segmented assimilation theory (1993) argues that the children of post-1965 immigrants do not all follow the classical upward path. Some assimilate into the white middle class; some experience downward mobility into a racialised urban underclass; others succeed through deliberate selective acculturation that preserves ethnic networks and language. Outcomes depend on race, parental human capital, and the mode of incorporation.
